display_content.code: """ TMI Formation Documents — single-library build with visual verification. Uses reportlab only. No post-processing. No external field injection. Fields added via pdfform during canvas construction. """ import subprocess, os from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas as rl_canvas from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib import colors from reportlab.lib.units import inch, pt from reportlab.pdfbase import pdfform from reportlab.platypus import ( SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, HRFlowable, KeepTogether, PageBreak, Flowable ) from reportlab.lib.styles import ParagraphStyle from reportlab.lib.enums import TA_CENTER, TA_LEFT, TA_JUSTIFY from reportlab.platypus.flowables import KeepTogether import io W, H = letter # 612 x 792 # ── Colours ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── BLUE = colors.HexColor("#1B3A6B") GOLD = colors.HexColor("#C9A84C") DARK = colors.HexColor("#1A1A1A") GRAY = colors.HexColor("#666666") LGRAY = colors.HexColor("#CCCCCC") WHITE = colors.white LM = RM = inch # left/right margin TM = BM = 0.9 * inch # top/bottom margin CW = W - LM - RM # content width = 468 pts # ── Styles — generous leading and spacing throughout ───────────────────────── def S(name, **kw): base = dict( fontName="Helvetica", fontSize=10, textColor=DARK, leading=16, spaceAfter=8, spaceBefore=0, leftIndent=0, rightIndent=0, alignment=TA_LEFT, ) base.update(kw) return ParagraphStyle(name, **base) ST = { # Cover "org": S("org", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=16, textColor=BLUE, alignment=TA_CENTER, leading=24, spaceAfter=6, spaceBefore=0), "org_sub": S("org_sub", fontName="Helvetica", fontSize=9, textColor=GRAY, alignment=TA_CENTER, leading=14, spaceAfter=14), "doc_title": S("doc_title", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=22, textColor=DARK, alignment=TA_CENTER, leading=32, spaceAfter=6, spaceBefore=14), "doc_sub": S("doc_sub", fontName="Helvetica-Oblique", fontSize=11, textColor=GRAY, alignment=TA_CENTER, leading=17, spaceAfter=20), # Body "body": S("body", fontName="Helvetica", fontSize=9.5, textColor=DARK, leading=15, spaceAfter=7, alignment=TA_JUSTIFY), "preamble": S("preamble", fontName="Helvetica-Oblique", fontSize=9.5, textColor=DARK, leading=15, spaceAfter=8, alignment=TA_JUSTIFY), # Headings "h1": S("h1", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=12, textColor=BLUE, leading=18, spaceBefore=18, spaceAfter=4), "h2": S("h2", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=10.5, textColor=BLUE, leading=16, spaceBefore=14, spaceAfter=4), "h3": S("h3", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=10, textColor=DARK, leading=15, spaceBefore=10, spaceAfter=3), # Scripture "scr_ref": S("scr_ref", fontName="Helvetica-BoldOblique", fontSize=9, textColor=BLUE, leading=14, leftIndent=20, spaceAfter=2, spaceBefore=8), "scr_text": S("scr_text", fontName="Helvetica-Oblique", fontSize=9, textColor=GRAY, leading=14, leftIndent=30, rightIndent=20, alignment=TA_JUSTIFY, spaceAfter=8), # Articles / sections "article": S("article", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=11, textColor=WHITE, alignment=TA_LEFT, leading=17, spaceAfter=8, spaceBefore=18), "section": S("section", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=9.5, textColor=DARK, leading=15, spaceBefore=10, spaceAfter=3), "confession":S("confession", fontName="Helvetica-BoldOblique", fontSize=9.5, textColor=DARK, leading=15, leftIndent=16, spaceAfter=6, spaceBefore=4, alignment=TA_JUSTIFY), # Lists "numbered": S("numbered", fontName="Helvetica", fontSize=9.5, textColor=DARK, leading=15, leftIndent=22, spaceAfter=4), "lettered": S("lettered", fontName="Helvetica", fontSize=9.5, textColor=DARK, leading=15, leftIndent=36, spaceAfter=3), # Signature area "sig_label": S("sig_label", fontName="Helvetica", fontSize=9, textColor=GRAY, leading=14, spaceAfter=2), # Footer "ft_org": S("ft_org", fontName="Helvetica-Bold", fontSize=8, textColor=BLUE, alignment=TA_CENTER, leading=12, spaceBefore=10, spaceAfter=2), "ft_line": S("ft_line", fontName="Helvetica", fontSize=8, textColor=GRAY, alignment=TA_CENTER, leading=12, spaceAfter=2), "ft_motto": S("ft_motto", fontName="Helvetica-Oblique", fontSize=8, textColor=GRAY, alignment=TA_CENTER, leading=12, spaceAfter=0), } # ── Flowable helpers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── def sp(h=8): return Spacer(1, h) def hr(c=LGRAY, t=0.5): return HRFlowable(width="100%", thickness=t, color=c, spaceAfter=6, spaceBefore=4) def gold_hr(): return HRFlowable(width="100%", thickness=1.5, color=GOLD, spaceAfter=10, spaceBefore=2) def P(text, style): return Paragraph(text, ST[style]) def cover(title, subtitle): return [ sp(24), P("THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE", "org"), gold_hr(), P("Austin, Texas · Established under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)", "org_sub"), P(title, "doc_title"), P(subtitle, "doc_sub"), hr(), sp(10), ] def h1(text): return [P(text, "h1"), gold_hr()] def h2(text): return [P(text, "h2"), hr(LGRAY, 0.4)] def scr(ref, text): return [P(ref, "scr_ref"), P(f'"{text}"', "scr_text")] class ArticleBanner(Flowable): def __init__(self, roman, title): Flowable.__init__(self) self.roman = roman self.title = title self.width = CW self.height = 26 def draw(self): c = self.canv # Background c.setFillColor(BLUE) c.rect(0, 0, self.width, self.height, fill=1, stroke=0) # Text — generous baseline so nothing clips c.setFillColor(WHITE) c.setFont("Helvetica-Bold", 10) label = f"ARTICLE {self.roman}" lw = c.stringWidth(label, "Helvetica-Bold", 10) c.drawString(10, 8, label) c.setFillColor(GOLD) c.setFont("Helvetica-Bold", 9.5) c.drawString(10 + lw + 8, 8, f"— {self.title}") def article(roman, title): return [sp(14), ArticleBanner(roman, title), sp(8)] def section(num, title): return P( f'Section {num}. {title}', "section") def ni(n, text): return P(f"{n}. {text}", "numbered") def li(l, text): return P(f"({l}) {text}", "lettered") def body(text): return P(text, "body") def confession(text): return P(text, "confession") def doc_footer(): return [ hr(), P("THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE", "ft_org"), P("Austin, Texas · 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)", "ft_line"), P("\"The one who is willing to work shall be equipped to work.\"", "ft_motto"), ] # ── Signature block (printed lines + field placeholders) ───────────────────── class SigBlock(Flowable): """ Draws printed signature lines with labels. fields: list of (label, line_width_fraction) Fields are spaced 48pt apart vertically. """ def __init__(self, fields): Flowable.__init__(self) self.fields = fields # [(label, width_fraction), ...] self.width = CW self.height = len(fields) * 52 + 10 def draw(self): c = self.canv y = self.height - 30 for label, wfrac in self.fields: line_w = self.width * wfrac # Label c.setFont("Helvetica", 8.5) c.setFillColor(GRAY) c.drawString(0, y + 14, label) # Signature line c.setStrokeColor(DARK) c.setLineWidth(0.5) c.line(0, y, line_w, y) y -= 52 def sig_block(fields): """fields: list of (label, width_fraction)""" return [sp(20), SigBlock(fields)] # ── Fillable field overlay — drawn on last page after platypus builds ───────── # We use a two-pass approach: # Pass 1: platypus builds the PDF, we count pages # Pass 2: we reopen with canvas and draw fields on the last page # This avoids any post-processing with a second library. # # Strategy: embed fields using a custom Flowable that writes pdfform fields # directly during platypus rendering. class FillableField(Flowable): """ A flowable that, when drawn, registers a pdfform text field at the current canvas position. """ def __init__(self, name, width, height=18, tooltip=""): Flowable.__init__(self) self.fname = name self.width = width self.height = height self.tooltip = tooltip def draw(self): c = self.canv pdfform.textFieldAbsolute( c, self.fname, 0, # x relative to flowable origin 0, # y relative to flowable origin self.width, self.height, self.tooltip ) def sig_row(label, field_name, width_frac=0.65, tooltip=""): """Returns a label paragraph + line + fillable field as a group.""" line_w = CW * width_frac return KeepTogether([ P(label, "sig_label"), HRFlowable(width=line_w, thickness=0.5, color=DARK, spaceAfter=1, spaceBefore=0), FillableField(field_name, line_w, 18, tooltip), sp(12), ]) # ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ # DOCUMENT 1 — THEOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK # ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ def build_framework(path): doc = SimpleDocTemplate(path, pagesize=letter, leftMargin=LM, rightMargin=RM, topMargin=TM, bottomMargin=BM, title="The Thessalonian Mandate Institute — Theological Framework", author="The Thessalonian Mandate Institute") s = [] s += cover( "THEOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK AND DOCTRINAL FOUNDATION", "A Comprehensive Defense of the Sacred Work Mandate") # PREAMBLE s += h1("PREAMBLE: THE NATURE OF THIS DOCUMENT") s.append(body("This document constitutes the foundational theological framework of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, a Faith-Based Organization established pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A). It serves simultaneously as a statement of doctrinal conviction, a declaration of sacred mission, and an authoritative defense of the theological mandate upon which this organization is built.")) s.append(body("This framework is not a legal argument. It is a theological confession. The authors of this document hold these positions not because they are convenient, but because they are true — true to the biblical text, true to the historical tradition of the Christian faith, and true to the urgent need of the present moment.")) s.append(body("Challenges to the sincerity or validity of this organization's theological basis are anticipated and addressed herein in full. No challenge has been left unanswered. Every doctrinal position stated in this document is grounded in scripture, supported by theological tradition, and demonstrated in practical mission.")) s.append(hr()) # PART I s += h1("PART I: THE SCRIPTURAL FOUNDATION") s += h2("1.1 The Primary Mandate — 2 Thessalonians 3:10") s.append(body("The doctrinal center of this organization is the explicit apostolic command recorded in Paul's second letter to the church at Thessalonica:")) s += scr("2 Thessalonians 3:10 (NIV)", "For even when we were with you, we gave you this rule: 'The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat.'") s.append(body("This verse is not a suggestion. It is not a cultural observation. Paul frames it explicitly as a rule — a binding apostolic directive given in person and now committed to writing for permanence. The Greek word used is παραγγέλλω (parangellō), the same term used for military orders. An organization that equips people to fulfill this obligation is not merely performing a social service — it is performing a ministry of obedience to divine command.")) s += h2("1.2 The Creation Mandate — Genesis 2:15 and Genesis 3:19") s += scr("Genesis 2:15 (NIV)", "The Lord God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it.") s += scr("Genesis 3:19 (NIV)", "By the sweat of your brow you will eat your food until you return to the ground.") s.append(body("Work precedes the Fall. In Genesis 2:15, God assigns Adam the task of tending and keeping the garden before sin enters the world. Work is therefore not punishment — it is the original vocation of humanity, established in the image of a God who himself worked in creation. The Fall does not eliminate the work mandate; it makes it harder. The sweat is new. The calling is not.")) s += h2("1.3 Excellence in Craft as Virtue — Proverbs 22:29") s += scr("Proverbs 22:29 (NIV)", "Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank.") s.append(body("The wisdom tradition of Israel elevates skilled work as the pathway to honor, influence, and dignity. The Hebrew word māhîr — skilled, swift, sharp, ready — describes mastery that comes only through deliberate practice. The cultivation of technical skill is a sacred pursuit. Training people in the crafts of the modern information economy is the active cultivation of māhîr in obedience to the wisdom mandate of scripture.")) s += h2("1.4 Labor as Worship — Colossians 3:23") s += scr("Colossians 3:23 (NIV)", "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters.") s.append(body("Every act of labor, performed with full devotion, becomes an act of worship. The secular and the sacred are not divided categories in Pauline theology — they are unified under the lordship of Christ. A displaced worker who learns a technical craft and builds products for human flourishing is, in the fullest theological sense, working for the Lord.")) s += h2("1.5 Preparation as Wisdom — Proverbs 24:27") s += scr("Proverbs 24:27 (NIV)", "Put your outdoor work in order and get your fields ready; after that, build your house.") s.append(body("Build capacity before building security. Develop productive ability before establishing stability. The deliberate work of equipping people with productive capacity is not merely practical advice — it is biblical wisdom in action.")) s.append(hr()) # PART II s += h1("PART II: THE HISTORICAL AND CONTEXTUAL FOUNDATION") s += h2("2.1 The Church at Thessalonica") s.append(body("Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia — a major Mediterranean seaport, a hub of trade, commerce, and skilled labor. The church Paul founded there consisted largely of manual laborers and working poor whose productive capacity was being disrupted by theological confusion. Some had stopped working, convinced the imminent return of Christ made continued labor unnecessary. Paul's rebuke uses the Greek ἀτάκτως — a military term meaning out of formation, undisciplined. The structural parallel to technological displacement is exact, not metaphorical.")) s += h2("2.2 Paul as a Working Minister") s += scr("2 Thessalonians 3:7–9 (NIV)", "We were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone's food without paying for it. On the contrary, we worked night and day, laboring and toiling so that we would not be a burden to any of you... in order to offer ourselves as a model for you to imitate.") s.append(body("Paul was a tent-maker who practiced his craft even during full-time apostolic ministry. He had the right to be supported by the church — he chose to work anyway, specifically so that his life would be a living argument for the theology he preached. An organization that trains others to work stands in direct apostolic succession to this tradition.")) s += h2("2.3 The Theological Tradition of the Work Mandate") s.append(body("Martin Luther recovered the doctrine of vocation (Beruf), arguing that every legitimate occupation is a divine calling. John Calvin extended this, holding that diligent labor in one's vocation is service to God and neighbor. Catholic social teaching insists on the dignity of labor and the right of workers to participate fully in economic life. Our mission represents the mainstream of Christian reflection on work, labor, and human dignity across five centuries of tradition.")) s.append(hr()) # PART III s += h1("PART III: THE DOCTRINAL POSITIONS OF THIS ORGANIZATION") for heading, text in [ ("On Scripture", "We believe the Holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments to be the inspired Word of God, authoritative in matters of faith and practice, and the ultimate standard against which all doctrine and action must be measured."), ("On the Nature of Work", "We believe that work is a divine institution, established by God before the Fall as the original vocation of humanity, and that the capacity for productive labor is a gift of God reflecting the image of the Creator in human beings."), ("On the Mandate to Work", "We believe that the apostolic command of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 constitutes a binding theological mandate: those who are able to work are obligated to work, and the community of faith has a corresponding obligation to equip those who are willing but lack the capacity to do so."), ("On Technological Displacement", "We believe that the mass displacement of workers by automation and artificial intelligence constitutes a spiritual crisis — a crisis of vocation — that demands a theological response, not merely a policy response."), ("On Technical Education as Ministry", "We believe that the work of equipping displaced workers with modern skills is a direct act of ministry. We do not merely provide job training. We restore human beings to the dignity of their God-given vocation."), ("On Excellence", "We believe that the standard of Proverbs 22:29 — skilled excellence that commands respect and opens doors — is the appropriate standard for all instruction offered by this organization."), ]: s.append(P(f"{heading}", "h3")) s.append(body(text)) s.append(hr()) # PART IV s += h1("PART IV: DEFENSE AGAINST ANTICIPATED CHALLENGES") for title, challenge, response in [ ("4.1 Challenge: This Organization Is a Pretext", "That this is a secular workforce program using religious language to obtain tax advantages.", "This challenge inverts the actual sequence. The theological conviction came first. The work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 is the origin and foundation — not a framing device applied to a pre-existing program. Furthermore, the 508(c)(1)(A) exemption exists precisely because the government recognizes that faith-based organizations operate from a different logic than secular nonprofits."), ("4.2 Challenge: The Theological Basis Is Thin", "That 2 Thessalonians 3:10 is read out of context, or that its connection to modern workforce development is a stretch.", "The scriptural foundation rests not on a single verse but on a convergent body of testimony across both Testaments — from Genesis through Proverbs through Colossians through Thessalonians. These constitute a coherent biblical theology of work recognized across the theological spectrum. The parallel to technological displacement is the natural application of an enduring principle to new material conditions. This is how Christian theology has always worked."), ("4.3 Challenge: Workforce Training Is Not Ministry", "That job training is a secular activity that cannot constitute genuine religious ministry regardless of framing.", "This challenge rests on a sacred-secular dualism that Colossians 3:23 explicitly demolishes. The Reformation doctrine of vocation holds that every legitimate occupation is a divine calling. A ministry that equips people to pursue their calling is performing the distinctly theological work of restoring human beings to their vocation. Paul's own practice as a tent-maker establishes that skilled technical work and genuine ministry are not merely compatible — they can be identical."), ]: s += h2(title) s.append(P(f"The anticipated challenge: {challenge}", "body")) s.append(P(f"The response: {response}", "body")) s.append(hr()) # PART V s += h1("PART V: THE CONTEMPORARY MISSION") s += h2("5.1 The Crisis of Technological Displacement") s.append(body("The current revolution in artificial intelligence and digital technology is displacing knowledge workers, clerical workers, and service workers at a scale and speed exceeding any previous technological transition in human history. The people most affected are not the wealthy and educated. They are the working class — people who built their lives around skills technology has now made obsolete. They are not lazy. They are not unwilling. They are displaced. They need equipping.")) s += h2("5.2 The Response of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute") s.append(body("The Institute provides instruction in technology fields with the highest demand and lowest barrier to entry for career changers: information technology support, cybersecurity, cloud computing, data analysis, and AI-assisted workflow management. These fields were selected according to the standard of Proverbs 22:29 — genuine skill that commands genuine respect, where mastery opens real doors.")) s += h2("5.3 The Measure of Our Success") s.append(body("We measure success not by enrollment numbers or revenue, but by the standard scripture sets: are those who complete our program equipped to fulfill the work mandate with excellence? Are they restored to the dignity of productive, purposeful, worshipful labor? This is the mission of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute — grounded in scripture, supported by tradition, demanded by the present moment, and pursued with the full conviction of sincere religious faith.")) s.append(hr()) s += h1("CONCLUSION: THE MANDATE STANDS") s.append(body("The theological foundation of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is not constructed — it is confessed. The work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 has stood for two thousand years. It stands now, in the age of artificial intelligence, with the same authority and the same demand: the one who is willing to work must be equipped to work. Here is the honest breakdown:

**The problem**

The bylaws say compensation for the Minister must be approved by disinterested Directors. When you are the sole Director and the Minister, there are no disinterested Directors. You are approving your own compensation, which is the textbook definition of a conflict of interest and the primary mechanism by which the IRS pierces private inurement claims against faith-based and nonprofit organizations.

**Why it is not fatal right now**

Two reasons:

First, the housing allowance is not technically compensation in the traditional sense — it is a tax exclusion on compensation already designated, not a payment the Board is authorizing out of operating funds. The IRS test for the parsonage exemption does not require disinterested Board approval the same way a salary does.

Second, you have zero revenue right now. There is nothing to pay yourself with. The conflict of interest problem becomes legally acute when actual money starts flowing. You have time to fix the structure before that happens.

**The fix**

Add a second Director before any compensation flows. That person does not need to be deeply involved in operations. They simply need to be a real person who genuinely affirms the Statement of Faith, attends Board meetings, and votes on your compensation as the disinterested party the bylaws require.

Your wife is the obvious candidate if she is willing. A trusted friend works. It does not need to be someone with organizational expertise — just someone real, present, and uncompensated.

We can still build it now. It should acknowledge the sole Director situation explicitly, establish a procedure for handling self-dealing transactions in the interim period before a second Director is appointed, and include a sunset provision requiring a second Director to be appointed before any compensation is paid.

That actually strengthens your position — it shows the organization anticipated the issue and built a governance response into its founding documents rather than ignoring it.

Want me to build it that way?

content.title: Form 202 Nonprofit Corporation - the Texas Secretary of State
content.text:
A nonprofit corporation is governed by titles 1 and 2 of the Texas Business Organizations Code (BOC). Title 1, chapter 3, subchapter A, of the BOC governs the formation of a nonprofit corporation and sets forth the provisions required or permitted to be contained in the certificate of formation. Nonprofit corporations may be incorporated for any lawful purpose. Corporations formed for the purpose of operating a nonprofit institution, including an institution devoted to a charitable, benevolent, religious, patriotic, civic, cultural, missionary, education, scientific, social, fraternal, athletic, or aesthetic purpose, may be formed and governed only as a nonprofit corporation under the BOC and not as a for- profit corporation. In a nonprofit corporation, no part of the income of the corporation may be distributed to a member, director or officer of the corporation.

The corporation shall make those documents available to the public for inspection and copying during regular business hours and may charge a reasonable fee for preparing a copy of those records. Failure to maintain those records, prepare an annual report or make the record or report available to the public is a Class B misdemeanor. These provisions do not apply to those corporations exempted under section 22.355 of the BOC. Also note that a nonprofit corporation supported in whole or in part by public funds or that spends public funds is considered a governmental body under chapter 552 of the Government Code (Public Information Act) and thus subject to the provisions of that Act regarding access to public information. In addition, a property owner’s association may also be subject to the Public Information Act pursuant to section 552.0035 of the Government Code. ... |Form 202 |[pic] |This space reserved for | |(Revised 12/21) |Certificate of Formation |office use.

Although consent is required, a copy of the person’s written or electronic consent need not be submitted with the certificate of formation. The liabilities and penalties imposed by sections 4.007 and 4.008 of the BOC apply with respect to a false statement in a filing instrument that names a person as the registered agent of an entity without that person’s consent. (BOC § 5.207) Office Address Requirements: The registered office address must be located at a street address where service of process may be personally served on the entity’s registered agent during normal business hours. Although the registered office is not required to be the entity’s principal place of business, the registered office may not be solely a mailbox service or telephone answering service (BOC § 5.201). • Article 3—Management: Except as provided by section 22.202 of the BOC, the affairs of a nonprofit corporation are governed by a board of directors.

This certificate of formation also may be used to create a nonprofit corporation that is managed solely by its members. If management of the corporation is to be vested in the nonprofit corporation’s members, a statement to that effect must be included in the certificate. If the nonprofit corporation is to be governed solely by its members, check the appropriate statement and proceed to Article 4 of this form. The fact that the individuals named on the board of directors are also members of the nonprofit entity does not mean that the corporation is governed by its members. Article 4—Members: If the corporation will not have members, the certificate of formation must include a statement to that effect. If management of the affairs of the corporation is vested in its members, you also must check statement A in Article 4 of this form. Checking statement B in Article 4 is inconsistent with a corporation that is managed by its members and will result in a rejection of the instrument.

If the corporation is not applying and distributing its property in accordance with section 22.304, the certificate of formation must include a statement describing the manner of distribution in the Supplemental Provisions/Information section of this form. If the space provided is not sufficient, an addendum may be included and attached to this form. Duration: Pursuant to section 3.003 of the BOC, a Texas nonprofit corporation exists perpetually unless provided otherwise in the certificate of formation. If formation of a corporation with a stated period of duration is desired, use the “Supplemental Provisions/Information” section of this form to provide for a limited duration. • Organizer: Only one organizer is required for the formation of a nonprofit corporation. An organizer may be any person having the capacity to contract for the person or for another; that is, a natural person 18 years of age or older, or a corporation or other legal entity.

You need this form when you want to turn an idea or existing unincorporated group into a Texas nonprofit corporation. It is the first legal step after choosing your name and governance approach.

Founders of community groups, charitable initiatives, religious ministries, educational programs, arts organizations, booster clubs, health initiatives, trade or professional associations, and neighborhood or property owners’ associations. Law firms, accountants, and consultants often prepare it for clients. Executive directors and board members may review and approve the content before filing. You need this form when you want to turn an idea or existing unincorporated group into a Texas nonprofit corporation. It is the first legal step after choosing your name and governance approach. If you intend to pursue tax-exempt recognition under federal or state law, you still start with this filing. Many exemptions and registrations ask for a file-stamped Certificate of Formation as proof that your organization exists and is authorized to operate. Typical usage scenarios include launching a new charity to run programs and accept donations, formalizing a youth sports league or arts collective 

This often means limiting the purpose to charitable, religious, educational, or similar activities and adding a clause that prohibits private benefit. You also include a dissolution clause directing assets to another qualifying entity or a public purpose. Place these provisions in the purpose and supplemental sections. Doing so avoids re-filing later. Finally, the certificate designates your registered agent, which ensures a reliable channel for official notices and legal papers. If your registered agent or registered office changes, you must update that information with a separate filing. Keeping this current protects your ability to receive critical notices and preserves due process. Approach the form in a sequence. You will move from name to governance to purpose to signatures. Keep your sentences short and your details precise. Here is a clear path through each section. You need your nonprofit’s proposed name, a Texas street address for your registered office, a consenting register

State a specific but flexible nonprofit purpose. Keep it clear and lawful. Examples include “The corporation is organized to support science education for youth in Texas” or “The corporation is organized to provide food assistance and related services to low-income families.” If you plan to seek federal tax-exempt status as a charitable or religious organization, add language that limits activities to exempt purposes and prohibits private benefit. You can include this limitation here or in the supplemental provisions. Avoid broad commercial language. Your purpose guides what you can do and how grantors view you. State whether the corporation will have members. Many nonprofits in Texas operate without statutory members. If you select “no members,” the board governs and elects directors. If you select “members,” your bylaws must define membership classes, rights, and voting.

You use Form 202 when you are creating a brand-new Texas nonprofit corporation. You complete it before you adopt bylaws, open a bank account, or sign major contracts. If you are converting from an informal group to a formal entity, you file Form 202 and then move your operations, contracts, and funds to the new corporation once formed. If you are running programs and taking donations under your personal name, you should file Form 202 as soon as you intend to hire, sign leases, or apply for grants. If your group is about to receive a large gift, secure a facility, or employ staff, forming first gives you a structural foundation and liability protection. When you plan to request corporate sponsorships or public grants, you will almost always need a filed formation certificate. If you operate a club or association with dues, events, or property, you use Form 202 to create a corporate home for those activities.

THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE
Founding Story and Minister Biography
=====================================


THE FOUNDING STORY
------------------

For eleven years, Rickey Jay Bennett II preached the Word of God on the streets
of America.

Not from a pulpit. Not with a salary or a congregation or a denominational
charter behind her. She preached from sidewalks and shelters and bus stations,
in cities from one coast to the other, as a traveling minister without
credentials or institutional backing — only a Bible and a conviction that would
not leave her alone.

The conviction was this: that work is sacred. That the capacity for productive,
skilled, dignified labor is not a feature of economic life but a feature of
human nature — given by a Creator God who worked in the beginning, before sin
entered the world, before the sweat and the thorns. That the man or woman who
is willing to work and cannot is not facing an economic problem. They are facing
a spiritual crisis. A violation of something God intended.

She knew this not because she had studied it in seminary. She knew it because
she was living it.

For twenty-three years, Rickey Bennett navigated homelessness, instability, and
the particular cruelty of a labor market that can strip a willing worker of
every foothold before they can find the next one. She lost jobs as quickly as
she found them. She preached the dignity of labor from the exact position of
someone the economy had left behind — not despite the contradiction, but because
of it. Because she understood from the inside what it means to be willing, to be
able, to be trying, and still to be without.

And then one day she put the book down.

Not with anger. Not with a declaration. She simply stopped picking it up. After
twenty-three years of living the problem and eleven years of preaching at it,
the gap between what the mandate promised and what the world delivered had
become too wide to keep standing in. The reassurance that God would provide had
grown hollow — not because it was false, but because provision requires more
than proclamation. It requires action. It requires someone to build the thing
that should have already existed.

The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is that thing.

It was not born in a boardroom or a seminary or a nonprofit incubator. It was
born in the understanding that the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 is not
a comfort. It is a command — and a command carries with it a corresponding
obligation. If those who are willing to work must work, then the community of
faith must ensure they have the capacity to do so. When technology displaces a
worker from their vocation, the Church does not get to offer thoughts and
prayers. The Church is obligated to equip.

Rickey Bennett built this organization because she spent two decades on the
other side of that obligation, waiting for someone to fulfill it. She is
building it so that the next generation of displaced workers does not have to
wait as long.

The mandate stands. Now we build.


MINISTER BIOGRAPHY — FORMAL VERSION
(For grant applications, official correspondence, and organizational materials)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Rickey Jay Bennett II is the Founder and Minister of The Thessalonian Mandate
Institute, a Faith-Based Organization established in Austin, Texas, under
26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A), dedicated to the workforce retraining of individuals
displaced by automation and artificial intelligence.

Minister Bennett brings to this work a singular combination of lived experience,
theological conviction, and organizational vision. An independent minister and
street preacher for over eleven years, she proclaimed the scriptural mandate of
dignified labor across the United States while navigating the very conditions of
economic displacement that the Institute exists to address. Her ministry was
conducted without institutional affiliation or denominational support —
grounded entirely in scripture and sustained by sincere religious conviction.

Her theological framework centers on the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10,
read within the broader biblical tradition of vocation that extends from the
creation mandate of Genesis 2:15 through the wisdom tradition of Proverbs and
the apostolic teaching of Paul. She understands technological displacement not
as an economic phenomenon but as a spiritual crisis — a forcible removal of
human beings from the vocation God assigned them at creation — and has
constructed a comprehensive doctrinal response to that crisis in the founding
documents of the Institute.

Minister Bennett is an independent researcher and writer whose work spans
artificial intelligence, philosophy of mind, and the theology of human labor.
She publishes under her legal name and has developed a body of theoretical work
addressing the intersection of technology and human dignity. Her approach to the
Institute's mission reflects both the rigor of her intellectual formation and
the urgency of her personal experience.

She serves as Minister, Chief Executive, Secretary, and Treasurer of the
Institute, and as the sole initial member of its Board of Directors.


MINISTER BIOGRAPHY — SHORT VERSION
(For website, press materials, and introductions)
--------------------------------------------------

Rickey Jay Bennett II is the Founder and Minister of The Thessalonian Mandate
Institute. She preached the dignity of labor on the streets of America for
eleven years — without a pulpit, without credentials, without institutional
backing — while navigating the same economic displacement her organization now
exists to address. She founded the Institute on the conviction that the work
mandate of scripture is not a comfort but a command, and that the community of
faith is obligated to equip those who are willing to work but cannot. She is
based in Austin, Texas.


NOTE ON IDENTITY
----------------

Minister Bennett is a transgender woman. This is stated plainly because plain
statement is the only treatment consistent with the dignity her organization
preaches.

The Institute serves anyone willing to work. Its minister is someone who has
spent a lifetime navigating a world that did not always make space for her —
which is precisely why she understands what it means to be displaced from your
vocation by forces beyond your control. Her identity is not incidental to the
mission. It is evidence that the mandate applies without exception, that dignity
in labor belongs to everyone the economy has left behind, and that the God who
commands work does not first require conformity.

The work is real. The theology is sound. The minister is who she is.

If you're running or volunteering with a workforce development nonprofit, you already know how critical grant funding is—and how frustrating it can be to find the right opportunities. You're competing for limited dollars while juggling program delivery, employer partnerships, and participant outcomes.

You need funding that aligns with your mission—whether that's job training, career coaching, apprenticeships, or reentry programs—but discovering those opportunities shouldn't feel like a second full-time job. Workforce development is a priority area for many federal, state, and corporate funders, but competition is steep. According to recent data, workforce-focused nonprofits represent a significant portion of the human services sector, which receives approximately 15–20% of all foundation grant dollars in the U.S. However, many workforce development organizations operate on budgets under $500K annually, meaning they're often competing with larger, more established nonprofits for the same pools of funding. Additionally, workforce grants frequently require demonstrated partnerships with employers, educational institutions, or government agencies—adding another layer of complexity to eligibility.

Unlike generic databases, Zeffy's tool is built specifically for small nonprofit teams. It lets you filter by mission area, location, deadline, and eligibility criteria—so you're not wading through thousands of irrelevant results. You'll see grants tailored to workforce training, job placement, skills development, and economic mobility. Free options like Grants.gov, your state's workforce development board, and community foundation websites are valuable but require manual searching and often lack user-friendly filters. Paid platforms like Candid (Foundation Directory) or GrantStation offer more comprehensive listings, but they can cost $100–$500+ annually. They're worth it if you're applying to 10+ grants per year, but many small teams find the ROI unclear—especially when results still require heavy filtering. When searching any database, prioritize these filters: Eligibility: Does the funder support workforce development specifically?

Mission alignment: Look for funders interested in job training, economic opportunity, career pathways, or populations you serve (e.g., justice-impacted individuals, youth, immigrants, veterans). Deadlines: Focus on grants with realistic timelines. If a deadline is two weeks away and requires extensive documentation, it may not be worth the effort. Geographic fit: Many workforce grants are state- or region-specific, tied to labor market data or local employer partnerships. One of the best ways to assess fit is to look at past grantees. If a funder has previously supported organizations similar to yours in size, mission, and geography, you're more likely to be a strong match. This information is sometimes available on funder websites or through 990 tax forms. Winning grants isn't just about finding them—it's about positioning your organization as a strong, credible partner.

ARMONK, N.Y., June 17, 2021 /PRNewswire/ -- At VivaTech today, IBM (NYSE: IBM) CEO Arvind Krishna announced a new collaboration with 30 global organizations including governments, community colleges, non-profits, and employment agencies, focused on helping underserved populations improve their skills and employability. According to the World Economic Forum, closing the global skills gap could add US$11.5 trillion to global GDP by 2028, but education and training systems need to keep pace with market demands. In addition, as reflected in a new study from the IBM Institute for Business Value (IBV), job seekers are facing big challenges, and one in four consumers surveyed globally plan to switch employers in 2021.

IDC believes that the partnerships IBM has announced are essential to helping meet the demands for tech jobs of the future. However, the partnership with ManpowerGroup is a perfect complement to IBM SkillsBuild's mission of providing training for to underrepresented groups as it provides meaningful career opportunities to badged IBM SkillsBuild participants," said Curtis Price, VP, Social, Environmental Responsibility and Ethics at IDC · About IBM SkillsBuild IBM SkillsBuild is a free, digital training program that helps adults develop valuable new skills and find jobs, regardless of their background or education. It operates in 141 countries, offering over 10,000 courses on cybersecurity, data analysis, cloud computing and many other technical disciplines — as well as in workplace skills such as Design Thinking. Participants can earn IBM-branded digital credentials and a global network of 90 nonprofit partners helps connect learners with local job opportunities.

This alliance will support IBM's goal to skill 500,000 people by the end of the year through the IBM SkillsBuild program. In addition, the collaboration will also collectively seek to: Provide 15,000 people with special program-based learning experiences, including personalized trainings, and the chance to apply for a job. Connect the workforce with real career opportunities, including a commitment to secure 7,000 jobs across different industries. "70% of employers can't find the skills they need for roles like data analytics, software development and remote customer service," said Jonas Prising, ManpowerGroup Chairman & CEO. "The only way we can address this acute talent shortage is through partnerships across business, government and education. That's why we are pleased to partner with companies like IBM who share our mission to create a more skilled and diverse workforce, so everyone is able to have a more equitable share of prosperity."

The collaboration spans 12 countries and includes ActionAid Italia Onlus, The American Indian Foundation Trust, Andhra Pradesh State Skill Development, Argencon, Bay Area Community College Consortium (BACCC), Bruxelles Formation, Cité des Métiers, CSC Academy, CSRBOX, Edunet Foundation, Fondazione Human Age Institute, Fundación Konecta, Junior Achievement Americas, Junior Achievement Italy, Laboratoria, Mission Locale de Paris, Reacha Foundation, Tata Community Initiatives Trust, The Royal Alberta College, Technifutur®, Technology Ireland ICT Skillnet, Training Point, Turkish Industry & Business Association (TÜSİAD), Unnati Foundation, Uvi Jagriti Sansthan, VetsinTech, Jeevitam-VSS Tech Solutions Pvt Ltd, Workforce Development Inc., and 60 000 rebonds. These organizations will leverage the online learning program IBM SkillsBuild with their members, mostly underserved populations such as veterans, women, minorities, refugees, and unemployed young adults.

content.title: IBM SkillsBuild: What It Is and How It Builds Essential Digital Skills
content.text:
When you complete learning paths or demonstrate specific skills, you earn IBM-branded digital badges and certificates that are recognised by employers globally. These aren't just participation certificates—they're verified credentials that ...

Job fairs, workshops, interview referrals, and potential internship opportunities create clear pathways from skill acquisition to actual employment. Through partnerships with platforms like Riipen, you can access project-based opportunities where employers recruit directly from successful graduates. Some collaborations even offer guaranteed interviews or structured recruitment pipelines for top performers, though these aren't universal across all programmes. This comprehensive approach addresses the common gap between learning something and actually landing a role that uses those skills. Success stories consistently show career changers and young professionals finding roles in: ... Many achieve this transition within that 3-6 month timeframe for highly motivated learners. For organisations looking to upskill their workforce or support their communities, IBM SkillsBuild solves several resource and scalability challenges simultaneously.

Community partnerships with nonprofits and advocacy groups serving underrepresented communities ... The job placement support extends to IBM's global network of employer partners who actively seek SkillsBuild-certified talent. These corporate partners participate in job fairs, skill competitions, and direct recruitment drives, with IBM itself directly considering badge holders for entry-level tech roles and facilitating internship opportunities for distinguished graduates. This connection between learning and actual job opportunities addresses one of the biggest frustrations with traditional online education—completing courses but struggling to translate that learning into employment. When you complete learning paths or demonstrate specific skills, you earn IBM-branded digital badges and certificates that are recognised by employers globally. These aren't just participation certificates—they're verified credentials that represent genuine skill attainment.

At IBM itself, earning SkillsBuild badges directly correlates to hitting performance targets and getting promoted more frequently. This creates a clear incentive loop that makes the learning feel genuinely valuable rather than just another box to tick. Enterprise-scale rollouts typically span 3-6 months for pilot phases, extending to 12-18 months for full global adoption depending on workforce size and localisation requirements. Successful implementations require coordination between: ... Executive sponsorship driving change management across regional training and communications programmes · The technical infrastructure for enterprise deployments centres on single sign-on (SSO) integration via SAML or OAuth protocols, enabling seamless access through existing corporate authentication systems. IBM SkillsBuild can operate as a co-branded or white-labelled microsite that sits within the organisation's broader learning ecosystem.

For organisations requiring advanced reporting, SkillsBuild supports integration with enterprise analytics solutions through standard data export mechanisms and open API connectivity, enabling sophisticated workforce development measurement and ROI calculations. What sets SkillsBuild apart from many online learning platforms is that completion rates consistently run above industry standards. Part of this success comes down to the digital badge system providing tangible proof of achievement. Unlike traditional training certificates that gather dust in filing cabinets, these badges become part of someone's professional identity. They go on LinkedIn profiles, get mentioned in job interviews, and create genuine pride in the learning journey. Badge portability ensures learners maintain ownership of their credentials across different platforms and career moves.

content.text: Clean on every page. Delivering it.

Ten pages. Sixteen pathways — six tech, seven non-tech, plus workplace readiness and English as a foundation that runs under everything.

A few things worth noting about what is in there:

The cohort model is framed as theological conviction, not operational preference — that framing matters for grant applications because it distinguishes the Institute from a generic online course referral service.

Every single pathway is zero cost to participants with confirmed free infrastructure behind it. The only asterisk is the Azure AZ-900 exam voucher at $165, which the Microsoft for Nonprofits program can cover.

IBM SkillsBuild is the single most important partnership to pursue immediately after the EIN is secured — they actively recruit nonprofit organizations and the Institute qualifies on every criterion they list.

The partnership pipeline section at the end is your first outreach list once you are operational.

What do you want to build next?

It is the nonprofit organization that coordinates the global domain name system — essentially the authority that decides what domain extensions exist, who can register them, and the rules registrars have to follow. Every domain on the internet ultimately traces back to ICANN's authority.

It was founded in 1998 and operates under a contract with the U.S. Department of Commerce, though it functions as an international body. It does not sell domains directly — it accredits registrars like Namecheap, GoDaddy, and Porkbun to sell them on its behalf under its rules.

If you want to keep using it, including all of the services associated with it (like a website or email service), you have to renew it with your registrar before it expires. The process of ensuring that your domain name registration stays current isn't complicated, but it's important to understand the process and your responsibilities before you are at risk of losing this valuable asset. Stay informed about your registrar's terms and conditions regarding your domain name's expiration, make payments associated with your domain name on time, and be sure to keep your contact information up to date with your registrar so that you receive updates and renewal reminders.

Internationalized Domain Name ,IDN,"IDNs are domain names that include characters used in the local representation of languages that are not written with the twenty-six letters of the basic Latin alphabet ""a-z"". An IDN can contain Latin letters with diacritical marks, as required by many European languages, or may consist of characters from non-Latin scripts such as Arabic or Chinese. Many languages also use other types of digits than the European ""0-9"".

The basic Latin alphabet together with the European-Arabic digits are, for the purpose of domain names, termed ""ASCII characters"" (ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange). These are also included in the broader range of ""Unicode characters"" that provides the basis for IDNs. The ""hostname rule"" requires that all domain names of the type under consideration here are stored in the DNS using only the ASCII characters listed above, with the one further addition of the hyphen ""-"". The Unicode form of an IDN therefore requires special encoding before it is entered into the DNS. The following terminology is used when distinguishing between these forms: A domain name consists of a series of ""labels"" (separated by ""dots""). The ASCII form of an IDN label is termed an ""A-label"". All operations defined in the DNS protocol use A-labels exclusively.

The Unicode form, which a user expects to be displayed, is termed a ""U-label"". The difference may be illustrated with the Hindi word for ""test"" — परीका — appearing here as a U-label would (in the Devanagari script). A special form of ""ASCII compatible encoding"" (abbreviated ACE) is applied to this to produce the corresponding A-label: xn--11b5bs1di. A domain name that only includes ASCII letters, digits, and hyphens is termed an ""LDH label"".

content.title: Can I buy a domain name forever? The truth about domain ownership
content.text:
The short answer is no, you can’t buy a domain forever, but you can register it for a set period, up to ten years at a time, and renew it to keep it active. Domain names work on a renewable registration system rather than permanent ownership.

Domain leasing refers to registering domain names for a fixed registration period rather than permanently owning them. When you register a domain, you gain the exclusive right to use that web address for a set time, usually between one and ten years. As long as you renew the registration before it expires, the domain remains under your control. You can think of it like renting an apartment. While you’re paying for it, you have the right to use the address and manage it as you see fit. The same applies to domain registration. You can claim the domain and connect it to a web hosting service for your website, email, or e-commerce store, regardless of the domain extension you choose, provided you continue renewing it. The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) is the nonprofit organization that oversees domain management on the Internet.

Here’s an overview of ICANN’s guidelines for owning a domain: Terms of domain registration: You can’t own a domain outright. Instead, you register or renew it for a predetermined period between 1 and 10 years before it expires. Domain registration through accredited registrars: Only accredited registrars can officially register and lease domain names. They are authorized to manage registrations and domain renewals, ensuring compliance with ICANN’s rules. Claims to domain use: Registering a domain grants you exclusive rights to use it, but it doesn’t make you the owner. If someone else claims it as their brand or trademark, you may lose the domain. To resolve these kinds of issues, use the Uniform Domain Name Dispute Resolution Policy (UDRP). You can also explore whether domain names are considered intellectual property to better understand how ownership and rights work.

Domains cannot be owned forever because the Domain Name System operates on renewable registrations rather than permanent ownership. ICANN limits how long a domain can be registered at one time to keep domain names available and fairly distributed. ICANN may periodically introduce new domain extensions to expand the available domain space. While the options expand, the number is still not infinite. ICANN ensures that no individual or business can permanently control the same domain name, giving others a fair chance to register it. In doing so, it: Prevents domain hoarding: Domain flippers often hold onto domains to sell them at a profit. The lease limit prevents them from acquiring too many, giving everyone the opportunity to register their desired domain without paying inflated fees. Promotes domain turnover: Regular lease renewals help return inactive or unused domains to the pool.

You can’t own a domain, but once you lease it for 1–10 years, it’s yours to use. To keep it active, you’ll need to renew your registration on time. If the renewal is missed, the domain gets deactivated. That means your website, email, and anything tied to it will stop working until it’s paid for. But that doesn’t mean you lose it right away. You’ve got 65 days to get it back: 30 days of grace, 30 days of redemption, and five days before deletion. After that, it’s released to the public for anyone to register. Can you buy a domain name forever? The short answer is no, you can’t buy a domain forever, but you can register it for a set period, up to ten years at a time, and renew it to keep it active. Domain names work on a renewable registration system rather than permanent ownership. This system keeps the internet fair by ensuring that unused names become available for others to register.

Confirmed and unchanged. The maximum registration period for any domain is ten years — a hard restriction set by ICANN. Any attempt to create a registration period longer than ten years will be rejected.

There is no workaround, no registrar that can override it, and no change on the horizon. Domains cannot be owned forever because the Domain Name System operates on renewable registrations rather than permanent ownership. ICANN limits registration periods to keep domain names available and fairly distributed.

In an effort to keep parishes from making bad domain choices in the future, I thought I'd share a few simple rules for choosing a new domain name for your parish: ... Let's be honest: Catholics in Baltimore are not going to have the patience to type out SaintMartinLoynazoftheAscensionCatholicChurchBaltimore.org just to find out what time Mass starts on Ash Wednesday. Yes, that might be the full name of the church, but is that how people refer to it? Go with something shorter: StMartinBaltimore.org. ... You want people to remember your domain name.

You want people to sit down at their computers and be able to type it in without Googling for it or flipping through your bulletin to find it. The easiest way to make a domain name memorable is to use something that connects with what people are already used to: Do people tell their friends they are attending Mass at Saint Teresa of Avila Catholic Church or just St. Teresa? I bet it's the latter, so use something like StTeresaMiami.org as your domain. Take note of how your parish typically writes the word "saint". Does your parish write out the full word or use the abbreviation? How it appears on your letterhead and sign out front should match how you spell it in your domain. Use words, not acronyms - unless the acronym is used frequently and consistently. If the folks at Most Holy Redeemer Parish commonly refer to the parish as MHR, then go ahead and use MHR in the domain name.

If parishioners have a common nickname for the parish, that might make a great domain choice - but don't try and force a new nickname. Trusted by non-profits, educators, and community-driven organizations for decades, a .org domain signals purpose and credibility to the audiences that matter most. The .org domain is one of the original extensions established during the early development of the internet, introduced in 1985. Derived from the word "organization," it was initially designed for non-profits and public interest groups that didn't fit within the .com or .net categories. Registration policies have evolved, and the extension is now open to anyone. Individuals, businesses, and institutions worldwide can register .org domains without restrictions. The Public Interest Registry (PIR) manages the extension under the oversight of the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN). Even with this broader accessibility, .org maintains a strong reputation for credibility and transparency.

The .org domain has been in use for almost 40 years. During this time, many of the world’s most respected and widely visited websites have chosen this extension, including Wikipedia.org, Mozilla.org, and the Red Cross. Its longstanding connection with credible, mission-focused institutions has helped build enduring public trust. For organizations that consider credibility a priority, this history provides a distinct and meaningful advantage. Unlike certain country code domains that require a local presence or specific documentation, .org domains are open to registrants worldwide. There are no eligibility criteria tied to geographic location, type of organization, or declared purpose. Whether you're registering a domain for a community initiative, an independent publication, a charitable foundation, or a business with a public mission, a .org domain can be secured without additional formal requirements.

    <div class="case-inner">
      <p class="section-label reveal">The Theological Foundation</p>
      <h2 class="section-title reveal">Why this organization exists.</h2>

      <div class="scripture-block reveal">
        <p class="scripture-text">"For even when we were with you, we gave you this rule: The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat."</p>
        <p class="scripture-ref">2 Thessalonians 3:10 (NIV)</p>
      </div>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        This verse is not a suggestion. The Greek word Paul uses — παραγγέλλω — is a
        military term for a binding command. Those who are able and willing to work
        are obligated to work. This has been the position of the Christian tradition
        from Paul through Luther through Calvin to the present day.
      </p>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        But the mandate has a second edge that the tradition has sometimes overlooked.
        If those who are willing to work must work, then the community of faith has a
        corresponding obligation: to ensure that those who are willing have the capacity
        to do so. When technology displaces a worker from their vocation, the Church
        does not get to offer thoughts and prayers. The Church is obligated to equip.
      </p>

      <div class="scripture-block reveal">
        <p class="scripture-text">"Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank."</p>
        <p class="scripture-ref">Proverbs 22:29 (NIV)</p>
      </div>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        This is the standard we hold ourselves to. We do not train people to barely
        qualify for entry-level positions. We train people to stand before kings —
        to carry credentials that employers actively seek, skills that genuinely
        transfer, and confidence that comes from genuine mastery.
      </p>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is not a charitable service with religious
        language applied to it. It is a ministry — an organization that understands
        workforce retraining as an act of obedience to divine command — and it operates
        with the theological rigor that obligation demands.
      </p>

<script>
function showPage(id) {
  document.querySelectorAll('.page').forEach(p => p.classList.remove('active'));
  document.getElementById(id).classList.add('active');
  window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'smooth' });
  if (id !== 'gateway') initReveal();
}

function scrollTo(id) {
  const el = document.getElementById(id);
  if (el) el.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'start' });
}

function initReveal() {
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach(entry => {
      if (entry.isIntersecting) {
        entry.target.classList.add('visible');
        observer.unobserve(entry.target);
      }
    });
  }, { threshold: 0.1 });

  document.querySelectorAll('.reveal').forEach(el => {
    el.classList.remove('visible');
    observer.observe(el);
  });
}

// Stagger reveal delays
document.querySelectorAll('.steps .step').forEach((el, i) => {
  el.style.transitionDelay = `${i * 0.1}s`;
});
document.querySelectorAll('.pathway-card').forEach((el, i) => {
  el.style.transitionDelay = `${(i % 4) * 0.08}s`;
});
</script>
</body>
</html>

  <section class="case-section" id="donor-case">
    <div class="case-inner">
      <p class="section-label reveal">The Theological Foundation</p>
      <h2 class="section-title reveal">Why this organization exists.</h2>

      <div class="scripture-block reveal">
        <p class="scripture-text">"For even when we were with you, we gave you this rule: The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat."</p>
        <p class="scripture-ref">2 Thessalonians 3:10 (NIV)</p>
      </div>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        This verse is not a suggestion. The Greek word Paul uses — παραγγέλλω — is a
        military term for a binding command. Those who are able and willing to work
        are obligated to work. This has been the position of the Christian tradition
        from Paul through Luther through Calvin to the present day.
      </p>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        But the mandate has a second edge that the tradition has sometimes overlooked.
        If those who are willing to work must work, then the community of faith has a
        corresponding obligation: to ensure that those who are willing have the capacity
        to do so. When technology displaces a worker from their vocation, the Church
        does not get to offer thoughts and prayers. The Church is obligated to equip.
      </p>

      <div class="scripture-block reveal">
        <p class="scripture-text">"Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank."</p>
        <p class="scripture-ref">Proverbs 22:29 (NIV)</p>
      </div>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        This is the standard we hold ourselves to. We do not train people to barely
        qualify for entry-level positions. We train people to stand before kings —
        to carry credentials that employers actively seek, skills that genuinely
        transfer, and confidence that comes from genuine mastery.
      </p>

      <p class="case-body reveal">
        The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is not a charitable service with religious
        language applied to it. It is a ministry — an organization that understands
        workforce retraining as an act of obedience to divine command — and it operates
        with the theological rigor that obligation demands.
      </p>
    </div>
  </section>

Absolutely possible. You already have the hardware. Running your own mail server is one of the oldest things you can do with a computer that stays on.

The software stack is free and well documented. Here is what it looks like:

---

**The components:**

**Postfix** — the mail transfer agent. Sends and receives email. The industry standard, free, runs on Linux and Windows via WSL.

**Dovecot** — the IMAP server. Lets you access your mailbox from any email client — Thunderbird, your phone, anything.

**SpamAssassin** — filters incoming spam. Free.

**Let's Encrypt SSL** — encrypts the connection. Same tool you are already using for the website. Free.

---

**The one real challenge:**

Your residential internet connection. Most ISPs block port 25 outbound — the port mail servers use to send email — specifically to prevent spam operations. This is the single most common obstacle to self-hosted email.

Two ways around it:

**Option A** — Call your ISP and ask them to unblock port 25. Some will do it, especially if you explain you are running a legitimate organization. It is worth asking.

**Option B** — Use a mail relay service for outbound delivery only. You run your own server for everything — storage, IMAP, incoming mail — but outbound mail routes through a relay. SendGrid, Mailgun, and Amazon SES all have free tiers sufficient for organizational email volume. You keep control of everything, you just use their outbound infrastructure.

---

**The deliverability issue:**

Even with port 25 open, email from a residential IP address will get flagged as spam by Gmail, Outlook, and others. The fix is three DNS records:

- **SPF** — tells the world which servers are authorized to send for your domain
- **DKIM** — cryptographically signs your outgoing mail
- **DMARC** — tells receiving servers what to do if SPF or DKIM fails

All three are free, configured in your DNS settings at your registrar. Without them your email will land in spam regardless of content.

---

**Realistic assessment:**

Setting this up properly takes a few hours and some patience. It is not beyond you — especially with me walking you through each step. Once it is running it is essentially maintenance-free and costs nothing beyond the domain you are already paying for.

Do you want me to write the complete setup guide for your specific situation — Windows machine, self-hosted, with the relay option as a fallback for outbound delivery?

chat_messages.text:
Good question. The answer is that you are not sending from port 25 — your email client is.

When you use Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, or any commercial email service, your client connects to **their** mail server on port 587 or port 465 — the submission ports — which are not blocked. Their server then handles the actual delivery to the recipient using port 25 on their end, from their data center IP address which is not on any residential block list.

So the flow is:

**Your computer → port 587 → Gmail's server → port 25 → recipient's server**

You never touch port 25. Gmail does. That is why it works.

When you run your own mail server the flow becomes:

**Your server → port 25 → recipient's server**

Now your residential IP is the one hitting port 25 outbound — and either your ISP blocks it, or the recipient's server sees a residential IP and flags it as likely spam.

The relay option solves this cleanly:

**Your server → port 587 → SendGrid/Mailgun → port 25 → recipient's server**

You keep full control of your server, your storage, your incoming mail, your IMAP — everything. You just hand the outbound leg to a service whose IP addresses are trusted. For the volume of a new organization that relay service is free.

So by 3:00 PM Monday you will have confirmed the name, and we can walk through the mail server setup whenever you are ready. The domain purchase and the server configuration can happen in the same session.

We configure it to use your Maildir storage " "and require encrypted connections.")) s.append(sp(6)) s.append(P("Edit the main Dovecot configuration:", "h3")) for c in [ "sudo nano /etc/dovecot/dovecot.conf", "", "# Find and set or add these lines:", "protocols = imap", "listen = *", ]: s.append(cmd(c)) s.append(sp(4)) s.append(P("Configure the mail location:", "h3")) for c in [ "sudo nano /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-mail.conf", "", "# Find mail_location and set it to:", "mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir", ]: s.append(cmd(c)) s.append(sp(4)) s.append(P("Configure authentication:", "h3")) for c in [ "sudo nano /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-auth.conf", "", "# Set these values:", "disable_plaintext_auth = yes", "auth_mechanisms = plain login", ]: s.append(cmd(c)) s.append(sp(4)) s.append(P("Configure SSL:", "h3")) for c in [ "sudo nano /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-ssl.conf", "", "# Set these values:", "ssl = required", "ssl_cert = Stop any services using port 80 temporarily:", "h3")) s.append(cmd("sudo systemctl stop nginx # if running")) s.append(sp(4)) s.append(P("Request the certificate:", "h3")) for c in [ "sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d mail.thessalonianmandate.org", "# Follow the prompts", "# Enter your email address when asked", "# Agree to terms of service", "# Certificate will be saved to /etc/letsencrypt/live/mail.thessalonianmandate.org/", ]: s.append(cmd(c)) s.append(sp(4)) s.append(P("Set up automatic renewal:", "h3")) for c in [ "sudo crontab -e", "# Add this line:", "0 12 * * * /usr/bin/certbot renew --quiet", "# This checks for renewal every day at noon", ]: s.append(cmd(c)) s.append(good("Certificates automatically renew every 90 days. For a mail server you need it running " "continuously. The reply should arrive."), ("Check mail logs for any errors", "sudo tail -50 /var/log/mail.log", "Look for any lines containing 'error' or 'reject'. Press Ctrl+C when done."), ("Verify SPF record", "# Visit mxtoolbox.com/spf.aspx", "Enter thessalonianmandate.org. Wait 30 minutes and try again."), ("Cannot connect IMAP from email client", [ "sudo systemctl status dovecot", "sudo journalctl -u dovecot --since '10 minutes ago'", ], "Most common cause is SSL certificate not yet issued. Complete Step 8 before connecting clients."), ("SSL certificate request fails", [ "# Verify your DNS A record is pointing to your current IP:", "curl ifconfig.me # Your current IP", "nslookup mail.thessalonianmandate.org # What DNS says", "# These must match before certbot will work", ], "If IPs do not match, update your A record at your registrar or wait for DNS propagation."), ("Server stops when Windows sleeps", [ "# In Windows Power Settings:", "# Set 'When plugged in, put the computer to sleep' to Never", "# Set 'When plugged in, turn off the display' to your preference", ], "A mail server cannot sleep. Configure Windows power settings to never sleep when plugged in."), ("Postfix or Dovecot not starting after reboot", [ "wsl -d Ubuntu -u root service postfix status", "wsl -d Ubuntu -u root service dovecot status", "wsl -d Ubuntu -u root service postfix start", ], "Run these from PowerShell or CMD. Your startup script should handle this automatically."), ] for title, commands, explanation in issues: items = [P(f"{title}", "h3")] for c in commands: items.append(cmd(c)) items.append(body(explanation)) items.append(sp(6)) s.append(KeepTogether(items)) s.append(hr()) # MAINTENANCE s += h1("ONGOING MAINTENANCE") s.append(body( "Once running, this server requires minimal maintenance. Here is what " "to do on a regular basis.")) s.append(sp(6)) for freq, task, command in [ ("Weekly", "Check mail logs for errors", "sudo tail -100 /var/log/mail.log | grep -i error"), ("Weekly", "Update Ubuntu packages", "sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y"), ("Monthly", "Check disk space — mail storage grows", "df -h"), ("Monthly", "Check certificate expiry", "sudo certbot certificates"), ("As needed", "Restart services after updates", "sudo systemctl restart postfix dovecot"), ("If IP changes", "Force DuckDNS update", "~/duckdns/duck.sh && cat ~/duckdns/duck.log"), ]: s.append(KeepTogether([ P(f"{freq} — {task}", "h3"), cmd(command), sp(6), ])) s.append(hr()) # SUMMARY s += h1("SUMMARY — YOUR COMPLETE MAIL INFRASTRUCTURE") summary = [ ("Mail Server Software", "Postfix (MTA) + Dovecot (IMAP) on Ubuntu/WSL2"), ("Hardware", "Ace Magic Kron1 Mini PC — 24GB RAM, 700GB storage"), ("Outbound Delivery", "SendGrid free relay — 100 emails/day, trusted IP addresses"), ("Dynamic DNS", "DuckDNS — updates every 5 minutes, free forever"), ("SSL Certificate", "Let's Encrypt — free, auto-renews every 90 days"), ("Email Addresses", "apply@thessalonianmandate.org, grants@thessalonianmandate.org"), ("IMAP Access", "Any device, anywhere — port 993, SSL/TLS"), ("Spam Filtering", "SpamAssassin — free, runs locally"), ("Authentication", "SPF + DKIM + DMARC — full deliverability stack"), ("Ongoing Cost", "$0 — domain registration is the only annual expense"), ("Auto-Start", "Starts with Windows via startup script"), ] for label, value in summary: s.append(cmd(f"{label:<28} {value}")) s.append(sp(12)) s.append(body( "This is a production-grade mail infrastructure that costs nothing to operate " "beyond the domain registration fee. It scales with the organization, stores " "your data on hardware you own, and gives you complete control over every " "aspect of your organizational communications.")) s += doc_footer() doc.build(s) print(f"Built: {PATH}") result = subprocess.run( ["pdftoppm", "-png", "-r", "120", PATH, "/tmp/mail"], capture_output=True, text=True) pages = sorted([f"/tmp/{f}" for f in os.listdir("/tmp") if f.startswith("mail-")]) print(f"Pages: {len(pages)}") print("Pages:", pages)

That is the natural next question once you have a minister track. If the Institute is training ministers it needs the authority to ordain them.

The short answer is you already have more authority to do this than you might think. As a 508(c)(1)(A) faith-based organization with a defined Statement of Faith and a designated minister, the Institute already has the theological standing to ordain. The question is not permission — it is credibility and process.

Here is how it works:

**Theologically** — ordination is the act of a faith community recognizing and setting apart someone for ministry. The Institute is a faith community. You are its minister. You can ordain. Full stop. No external body has to approve this. That is the First Amendment operating exactly as intended.

**Practically** — for the ordination to carry weight it needs a documented process. A theological examination against the Statement of Faith. A period of supervised ministry. content.text:
Less transparency often leads to increased utility for NPOs, but more transparency can increase NPOs’ utility if the information available exceeds a certain threshold. Fluctuating donations are challenging for NPOs’ planning and may impact administrative capacities negatively.

## Introduction

Private donors face an ever growing number of organizations asking for their support and have to decide on whom to donate to (Kovács and Spens [12]). Donors cannot readily obtain information about whether organizations use their funds in the way the donors intend or do so in the most efficient way. Benchmarks are a tool for assessing the performance of an NPO, well suited to support the decision making process of the donor. An easily accessible and widely used benchmark is the ratio overhead costs relative to total expenses, since these numbers can be extracted from publicly available accounting information. 

From this viewpoint, the development of the “Nonprofit Starvation Cycle” (Lecy and Searing [13]) can be considered as a foreseeable development: Triggered by donor expectation concerning ‘acceptable’ overhead ratios and NPO rating organizations publishing benchmarks based on overhead ratios, donors reward low ratios by donating more to seemingly ‘efficient’ NPOs. This lures NPOs into decreasing the ratio of overhead to gain a competitive advantage in donation ‘markets’, further elevating donor pressure by increasingly unrealistic expectations. At some point, overhead costs can only be decreased by choosing between reducing necessary administrative capacities or engaging in misreporting on overhead used as a misleading tactic to succeed in this price war turned into a race to the bottom (Lecy and Searing [13]).
